title: Defanging an IP Address
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the defanged version of an IPv4 address by replacing each period with [.] .
Idea: Replace each literal period with `[.]` in the address string.
Technique and why it applies: A direct period replacement preserves the address while making each separator non-clickable as a dot.
Invariant: Every input period is replaced and all other characters retain their original order.
Edge cases: IPv4 input has four numeric components and three periods; the replacement is textual and does not parse numeric ranges.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code:
class Solution:
 def defangIPaddr(self,address):return address.replace('.','[.]')
complexity_reason: A direct period replacement preserves the address while making each separator non-clickable as a dot.

title: Relative Sort Array
approach_name: Count priority values then sort the remainder
notes:
Task and constraints: Sort arr1 so values appearing in arr2 follow arr2’s order, while other values appear in ascending order at the end.
Idea: Count occurrences of each value in `arr1`, emit values in the order listed by `arr2`, then append all remaining values in ascending order.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counts preserve multiplicities while `arr2` supplies the priority order and sorting handles values absent from it.
Invariant: The count map tracks exactly how many copies remain to emit; each `arr2` value is exhausted before the sorted remainder is appended.
Edge cases: Values repeated in `arr1` must be emitted with full multiplicity; `arr2` values are unique under the problem constraints.
Complexity: O(n+m+u log u) time when sorting u remaining distinct values and O(n+u) space.
complexity_reason: Frequency counts preserve multiplicities while `arr2` supplies the priority order and sorting handles values absent from it.

title: Relative Sort Array
approach_name: Count priority values then sort the remainder
notes:
Task and constraints: Sort arr1 so values appearing in arr2 follow arr2’s order, while other values appear in ascending order at the end.
Idea: Count occurrences of each value in `arr1`, emit values in the order listed by `arr2`, then append all remaining values in ascending order.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counts preserve multiplicities while `arr2` supplies the priority order and sorting handles values absent from it.
Invariant: The count map tracks exactly how many copies remain to emit; each `arr2` value is exhausted before the sorted remainder is appended.
Edge cases: Values repeated in `arr1` must be emitted with full multiplicity; `arr2` values are unique under the problem constraints.
Complexity: O(n+m+u log u) time when sorting u remaining distinct values and O(n+u) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int[] relativeSortArray(int[] arr1,int[] arr2){Map<Integer,Integer>c=new HashMap<>();for(int x:arr1)c.put(x,c.getOrDefault(x,0)+1);int[]out=new int[arr1.length];int i=0;for(int x:arr2){int n=c.getOrDefault(x,0);while(n-->0)out[i++]=x;c.remove(x);}List<Integer>rest=new ArrayList<>();for(Map.Entry<Integer,Integer>e:c.entrySet())for(int j=0;j<e.getValue();j++)rest.add(e.getKey());Collections.sort(rest);for(int x:rest)out[i++]=x;return out;} }
complexity_reason: Frequency counts preserve multiplicities while `arr2` supplies the priority order and sorting handles values absent from it.

title: Number of Equivalent Domino Pairs
notes:
Task and constraints: Count pairs of dominoes equivalent under swapping their two values.
Idea: Canonicalize each domino as `(min(a,b), max(a,b))` or an equivalent fixed key and count how many previous dominoes share that key.
Technique and why it applies: Canonicalizing both orientations to the same key turns equivalence into a frequency-counting problem.
Invariant: The running answer adds the number of earlier equivalent dominoes, so each unordered pair is counted once at its later occurrence.
Edge cases: Reversing a domino's two values does not change its key; duplicate dominoes form multiple pairs.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Canonicalizing both orientations to the same key turns equivalence into a frequency-counting problem.

title: Number of Equivalent Domino Pairs
notes:
Task and constraints: Count pairs of dominoes equivalent under swapping their two values.
Idea: Canonicalize each domino as `(min(a,b), max(a,b))` or an equivalent fixed key and count how many previous dominoes share that key.
Technique and why it applies: Canonicalizing both orientations to the same key turns equivalence into a frequency-counting problem.
Invariant: The running answer adds the number of earlier equivalent dominoes, so each unordered pair is counted once at its later occurrence.
Edge cases: Reversing a domino's two values does not change its key; duplicate dominoes form multiple pairs.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int numEquivDominoPairs(int[][] dominoes){Map<Integer,Integer>c=new HashMap<>();int ans=0;for(int[]d:dominoes){int a=Math.min(d[0],d[1]),b=Math.max(d[0],d[1]),key=a*10+b;ans+=c.getOrDefault(key,0);c.put(key,c.getOrDefault(key,0)+1);}return ans;} }
complexity_reason: Canonicalizing both orientations to the same key turns equivalence into a frequency-counting problem.

title: N-th Tribonacci Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Return Tn where T0=0, T1=T2=1, and each later term is the sum of the previous three.
Idea: Maintain the last three Tribonacci values and update the triple by summing them until reaching index `n`.
Technique and why it applies: Only the previous three terms are needed, so rolling variables avoid a full dynamic-programming array.
Invariant: The rolling variables always hold the three most recent terms needed for the next recurrence.
Edge cases: Return the base values directly for n=0, 1, or 2; later values depend on the previous three.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Only the previous three terms are needed, so rolling variables avoid a full dynamic-programming array.

title: N-th Tribonacci Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Return Tn where T0=0, T1=T2=1, and each later term is the sum of the previous three.
Idea: Maintain the last three Tribonacci values and update the triple by summing them until reaching index `n`.
Technique and why it applies: Only the previous three terms are needed, so rolling variables avoid a full dynamic-programming array.
Invariant: The rolling variables always hold the three most recent terms needed for the next recurrence.
Edge cases: Return the base values directly for n=0, 1, or 2; later values depend on the previous three.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
code: class Solution { public int tribonacci(int n){int a=0,b=1,c=1;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){int d=a+b+c;a=b;b=c;c=d;}return a;} }
complexity_reason: Only the previous three terms are needed, so rolling variables avoid a full dynamic-programming array.

title: Day of the Year
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the one-based day number within the year for a date formatted YYYY-MM-DD.
Idea: Parse year, month, and day; sum the lengths of all preceding months and add the day, including February's leap-day adjustment when applicable.
Technique and why it applies: Summing month lengths before the given month converts a valid calendar date to its ordinal day.
Invariant: The accumulator equals the one-based ordinal day after adding every complete earlier month and the current date's day.
Edge cases: Leap years include February 29; dates are valid Gregorian dates; January dates require no preceding-month additions.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space for a fixed 12-month calendar.
complexity_reason: Summing month lengths before the given month converts a valid calendar date to its ordinal day.

code: class Solution { public int dayOfYear(String date){int y=Integer.parseInt(date.substring(0,4)),m=Integer.parseInt(date.substring(5,7)),d=Integer.parseInt(date.substring(8,10));int[]days={31,28,31,30,31,30,31,31,30,31,30,31};if(java.time.Year.isLeap(y))days[1]=29;for(int i=0;i<m-1;i++)d+=days[i];return d;} }
complexity_reason: Summing month lengths before the given month converts a valid calendar date to its ordinal day.

title: Find Words That Can Be Formed by Characters
approach_name: Check word counts against available characters
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of lengths of words that can be formed from chars using each character no more often than it appears there.
Idea: Count available character frequencies once; for each word, count its letters and accept it only if no letter demand exceeds the available count.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing per-letter frequencies enforces character multiplicities, not just membership in the allowed set.
Invariant: The availability counts remain unchanged across candidate words, while each word's local counts verify that its letters can be supplied.
Edge cases: Repeated letters consume repeated copies; rejected words contribute zero length; accepted words contribute their entire length.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(1) alphabet space per word beyond the input.
complexity_reason: Comparing per-letter frequencies enforces character multiplicities, not just membership in the allowed set.

title: Find Words That Can Be Formed by Characters
approach_name: Check word counts against available characters
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of lengths of words that can be formed from chars using each character no more often than it appears there.
Idea: Count available character frequencies once; for each word, count its letters and accept it only if no letter demand exceeds the available count.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing per-letter frequencies enforces character multiplicities, not just membership in the allowed set.
Invariant: The availability counts remain unchanged across candidate words, while each word's local counts verify that its letters can be supplied.
Edge cases: Repeated letters consume repeated copies; rejected words contribute zero length; accepted words contribute their entire length.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(1) alphabet space per word beyond the input.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int countCharacters(String[] words,String chars){int[]have=new int[26];for(char c:chars.toCharArray())have[c-'a']++;int ans=0;for(String w:words){int[]need=new int[26];for(char c:w.toCharArray())need[c-'a']++;boolean ok=true;for(int i=0;i<26;i++)if(need[i]>have[i]){ok=false;break;}if(ok)ans+=w.length();}return ans;} }
complexity_reason: Comparing per-letter frequencies enforces character multiplicities, not just membership in the allowed set.

title: Compare Strings by Frequency of the Smallest Character
approach_name: Sort word frequencies and upper-bound queries
notes:
Task and constraints: For each query, count words whose frequency of their smallest character is strictly greater than the query’s corresponding frequency.
Idea: Compute each word's frequency of its smallest character, sort those frequencies, and use an upper-bound search to count values strictly greater than each query frequency.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting the word frequencies makes each strict-greater-than query answerable by binary search.
Invariant: The sorted frequency array lets binary search locate the first value greater than the query; the suffix length is the answer.
Edge cases: The comparison is strict, so equal frequencies do not count; words are non-empty lowercase strings.
Complexity: O(W log W + Q log W + total characters) time and O(W) space.
complexity_reason: Sorting the word frequencies makes each strict-greater-than query answerable by binary search.

title: Compare Strings by Frequency of the Smallest Character
approach_name: Sort word frequencies and upper-bound queries
notes:
Task and constraints: For each query, count words whose frequency of their smallest character is strictly greater than the query’s corresponding frequency.
Idea: Compute each word's frequency of its smallest character, sort those frequencies, and use an upper-bound search to count values strictly greater than each query frequency.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting the word frequencies makes each strict-greater-than query answerable by binary search.
Invariant: The sorted frequency array lets binary search locate the first value greater than the query; the suffix length is the answer.
Edge cases: The comparison is strict, so equal frequencies do not count; words are non-empty lowercase strings.
Complexity: O(W log W + Q log W + total characters) time and O(W) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int[] numSmallerByFrequency(String[] queries,String[] words){int[]a=new int[words.length];for(int i=0;i<words.length;i++)a[i]=f(words[i]);Arrays.sort(a);int[]out=new int[queries.length];for(int i=0;i<queries.length;i++){int x=f(queries[i]),l=0,r=a.length;while(l<r){int m=(l+r)/2;if(a[m]<=x)l=m+1;else r=m;}out[i]=a.length-l;}return out;}private int f(String s){char c='z';for(char x:s.toCharArray())if(x<c)c=x;int n=0;for(char x:s.toCharArray())if(x==c)n++;return n;} }
complexity_reason: Sorting the word frequencies makes each strict-greater-than query answerable by binary search.

title: Distance Between Bus Stops
notes:
Task and constraints: Given a circular route with distances between adjacent stops, return the shorter distance between start and destination.
Idea: Sum distances along the clockwise segment between the two indices and subtract that sum from the total route length to obtain the opposite direction; return the smaller distance.
Technique and why it applies: The shorter circular route is the minimum of one arc sum and total distance minus that arc.
Invariant: The two candidate distances cover the two arcs of the circular route and add up to the total distance.
Edge cases: Start and destination may be given in either order; distances are nonnegative; the shorter of the two directions is required.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The shorter circular route is the minimum of one arc sum and total distance minus that arc.

title: Distance Between Bus Stops
notes:
Task and constraints: Given a circular route with distances between adjacent stops, return the shorter distance between start and destination.
Idea: Sum distances along the clockwise segment between the two indices and subtract that sum from the total route length to obtain the opposite direction; return the smaller distance.
Technique and why it applies: The shorter circular route is the minimum of one arc sum and total distance minus that arc.
Invariant: The two candidate distances cover the two arcs of the circular route and add up to the total distance.
Edge cases: Start and destination may be given in either order; distances are nonnegative; the shorter of the two directions is required.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int distanceBetweenBusStops(int[] distance,int start,int destination){if(start>destination){int t=start;start=destination;destination=t;}int clockwise=0,total=0;for(int x:distance)total+=x;for(int i=start;i<destination;i++)clockwise+=distance[i];return Math.min(clockwise,total-clockwise);} }
complexity_reason: The shorter circular route is the minimum of one arc sum and total distance minus that arc.

title: Day of the Week
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the weekday name for a valid Gregorian date in the supported year range.
Idea: Use the provided calendar library or a fixed Gregorian day-offset calculation to map the valid date to its weekday name.
Technique and why it applies: A calendar calculation accounts for leap years and varying month lengths more reliably than hand-written weekday guesses.
Invariant: The computed date offset determines a single weekday in the repeating seven-day cycle.
Edge cases: The supported dates are valid Gregorian dates; weekday names must match the required English labels.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space for a bounded supported date range.
complexity_reason: A calendar calculation accounts for leap years and varying month lengths more reliably than hand-written weekday guesses.

title: Minimum Absolute Difference
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all pairs with the minimum absolute difference in an array, with each pair sorted and the list in ascending order.
Idea: Sort the array, scan adjacent values to find the smallest difference, then collect every adjacent pair attaining that difference.
Technique and why it applies: Adjacent sorted pairs contain every possible minimum gap, reducing the pair search to a linear scan after sorting.
Invariant: In sorted order, a minimum absolute difference must occur between adjacent elements, so nonadjacent pairs need not be checked.
Edge cases: Duplicate values produce difference zero; each returned pair is ordered ascending and the result list follows sorted order.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for sorting/output depending on sort implementation.
complexity_reason: Adjacent sorted pairs contain every possible minimum gap, reducing the pair search to a linear scan after sorting.

title: Minimum Absolute Difference
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all pairs with the minimum absolute difference in an array, with each pair sorted and the list in ascending order.
Idea: Sort the array, scan adjacent values to find the smallest difference, then collect every adjacent pair attaining that difference.
Technique and why it applies: Adjacent sorted pairs contain every possible minimum gap, reducing the pair search to a linear scan after sorting.
Invariant: In sorted order, a minimum absolute difference must occur between adjacent elements, so nonadjacent pairs need not be checked.
Edge cases: Duplicate values produce difference zero; each returned pair is ordered ascending and the result list follows sorted order.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for sorting/output depending on sort implementation.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<List<Integer>> minimumAbsDifference(int[] arr){Arrays.sort(arr);int d=Integer.MAX_VALUE;for(int i=0;i<arr.length-1;i++)d=Math.min(d,arr[i+1]-arr[i]);List<List<Integer>>out=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<arr.length-1;i++)if(arr[i+1]-arr[i]==d)out.add(Arrays.asList(arr[i],arr[i+1]));return out;} }
complexity_reason: Adjacent sorted pairs contain every possible minimum gap, reducing the pair search to a linear scan after sorting.
